spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty and recorded by his disciple Guanding: the general outline has already been explained above.
Furthermore, for what reasons are the names "calm abiding" (*śamatha*) and "insight" (*vipaśyanā*) established?
Briefly, there are four:
first, their mutual dependence.
Second, transcending dependence;
third, reconciling differences;
fourth, penetrating the three virtues.
First, regarding mutual dependence:
cessation (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) each have three meanings, including the meaning of "stopping" (*śama*).
The meaning of "stopping" (*sthāpana*). In contrast to the meaning of not stopping, it has the sense of "resting. As for the meaning of "cessation" (*śamana*):
All evil discursive thoughts, false recollections, and mental conceptions were stilled and brought to rest.
Vimalakīrti asked:
"What is meant by 'clinging to objects'?"
This refers to taking the three realms as objects.
What is meant by "ceasing the grasping of objects"?
It means that the mind finds nothing to be apprehended.
This is named according to that which is to be eliminated;
it carries the meaning of cessation.
As for the meaning of "stopping":
The mind, conditioned by the principle of reality, maintains mindfulness that is present, stable, and immovable.
As the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states:
"The prajñā that enters into principle is called 'abiding' (*sthiti*)."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"By means of the dharma of non-abiding, one abides within the *prajñāpāramitā*.
This is so named because it is capable of bringing cessation.
This is the meaning of cessation.
While the phrasing regarding "cessation" as opposed to "non-cessation" may apply generally to what precedes, the intended meaning is fundamentally distinct.
Why is this? The two preceding types of cessation correspond to the flux of birth and death;
they are discussed as "cessation" in reference to nirvana.
The mental activities that lie outside of principle are discussed in terms of cessation according to the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
This [previous discussion] was a general discourse on the mutual dependence of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*);
now, we specifically discuss their mutual dependence according to the theory of the truths (*satya*).
Ignorance is itself the dharma-nature, and the dharma-nature is itself ignorance.
Ignorance is neither ceasing nor non-ceasing, yet it is called "non-ceasing";
the dharma-nature is neither ceasing nor non-ceasing, yet it is called "ceasing."
This is not merely a cessation relative to ignorance;
it is called the cessation of the dharma-nature itself.
As the sutra says: "The dharma-nature is neither born nor extinguished."
While it is said that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is quiescent,
the nature of phenomena is neither defiled nor pure;
yet it is also said that the nature of phenomena is pure.

The meaning of "contemplation" (vipaśyanā) is the sense of penetrating through; it is contrasted with the meaning of non-contemplation.
As for the meaning of "penetration" (pratividh), it is...
Wisdom utilizes penetration to extinguish afflictions.
A Great Sūtra says:
"A sharp pickaxe cleaves the earth, through bedrock, sand, and gravel, all the way down to the diamond layer."
The Lotus Sūtra says:
"One may dig and excavate a high plateau and still encounter dry soil;
yet if one does not cease exerting effort, one will eventually reach the mud."
This is established as the "pervasive contemplation" (vyavacāraṇa) based on the name derived from that which is to be refuted.
Regarding the meaning of "contemplative penetration": it means that the wisdom of contemplation penetrates and accords with suchness (tathatā).
The *Śūramgama-samādhi-sūtra* (Shuìyìng) states:
"One who has stilled the mind and reached the fundamental source is therefore called a śramaṇa.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàlùn) states:
When the pure mind is always one-pointed,
one is then able to see prajñā;
this is named according to that which is capable of contemplation.
Therefore, the "view of thorough penetration" (prativedha-darśana) is established.
As for the contrast between "not viewing" and "viewing," although the phrasing is consistent with what precedes, the underlying meaning is fundamentally distinct.
The two preceding contemplations also pertain to both birth-and-death and to penetrating through them in their extreme density;
they pertain to the realization of contemplation regarding confusion and blindness.
These are generally explained as the mutual relationship between wisdom and abandonment, clarifying the nature of contemplation.
Now, to distinguish this according to the principle of the Truths:
ignorance is itself the dharma-nature, and the dharma-nature is itself ignorance.
Ignorance is neither contemplation nor non-contemplation.
Ignorance is called "non-contemplation," yet the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is neither contemplation nor non-contemplation; nevertheless,
the nature of phenomena is called "contemplation."
As a sutra says:
"The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is neither light nor darkness,
yet we call the nature of phenomena 'light.'"
The emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is neither wisdom nor ignorance;
yet, to designate this emptiness of the ultimate truth as "wisdom" is to clarify "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) in contrast to "non-contemplation."
Therefore, *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) each derive their names from three meanings.
Second, regarding the elucidation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as being beyond relative dependence:
this refers to the sublation of the aforementioned three types of relative *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
First, it is refuted horizontally;
next, it is refuted vertically.
If cessation were named solely after that which is ceased, [it would follow that]...
Illuminating the object is primary, while the elimination of afflictions is secondary.
Since the name is derived from that which is abandoned,
if the name were applied based on what is secondary, it would immediately fall into the fault of being of another nature.
If [the name] "cessation" were derived from its capacity to destroy [afflictions],
then illuminating the object would be primary while the elimination of delusions would be secondary.
Since it is said that the name "capable of illuminating" arises from wisdom (*jñāna*), it would then fall into the error of [imputing] intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It is not because of the cessation of deluded thoughts that there is stilling;
it is not because of abiding in principle that there is stilling;
it is because of the exhaustion of the causes and conditions of wisdom that there is stilling.
If names arise from conjunction, one falls into the error of commonality (*sādhāraṇa*).
If it is neither that which is refuted nor that which refutes, yet one speaks of "cessation," this falls into the error of causelessness (*ahetutva*).
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said:
"All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another;
they do not arise from both, nor are they without cause; therefore, they are said to be unarisen."
How could the names "non-arising śamatha-vipaśyanā" be established through the four propositions?
Names established by means of the four propositions arise from mutual dependence;
they are conceivable and expressible.
These fetters and afflictions arise as that which can be broken and destroyed;
they are births characterized by arising, ceasing, and flux.
What, then, is meant by "stopping"?
Regarding the birth of delusion and perversion:
what is meant by "penetrative observation"?
Furthermore, as for "vertical refutation":
If it arises from the four propositions,
it is merely "arising of arising" and not cessation or contemplation.
If one can bring to rest the views and afflictions and abide in the ultimate truth, [then it is true cessation and contemplation].
This is the explanation of the arising and non-arising of dependent origination in terms of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
If one enters the provisional through the emptiness of mind,
one brings to rest the sands of phenomena and abides in the conventional truth.
This refers to the non-arising of that which was expected to arise;
it is the description of the śamatha and vipaśyanā of the non-arising of arising.
If one brings stillness to ignorance and halts it within the principle of the mind, [this is achieved].
This refers merely to the discussion of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as they relate to the two extremes of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa;
all such [discussions] involve mutual dependence and are within the realm of the conceivable.
The fetters and delusions that have arisen can be destroyed;
how much more so when they have not yet arisen? How much more so when they do not arise at all?
It is already not [a state of] contemplation for oneself, let alone being without contemplation.
Why is this? Because the grasping [of signs] has not been completely eliminated,
and because the path of speech has not been severed.
Because the fruits of karma are never severed,
what is now called "severing dependencies" refers to the cessation of all horizontal and vertical dependencies.
It transcends all conceptual thought;
it transcends all afflictions, karmas, and fruits;
and it transcends all teachings, contemplations, realizations, and so forth.
Because nothing at all arises, it is called "stopping" (śamatha).
Stopping itself is also unattainable.
Contemplation (vipaśyanā) is darkly quiescent like its object; since the object is already extinguished and pure.
If even purity does not exist, how can there be contemplation?
Since both tranquility and contemplation do not exist,
how can one speak of tranquility and contemplation by depending on their non-cessation?
In reliance upon cessation and contemplation, one speaks of neither cessation nor contemplation;
in reliance upon cessation and non-cessation, one speaks of neither cessation nor non-cessation.
Thus, one knows that both cessation and non-cessation are ultimately unattainable.
Neither ceasing nor not ceasing, it is likewise unattainable.
Since all oppositions and relativity have been severed, it is not conditioned;
it cannot be conceived through the four logical alternatives.
Therefore, it is not that words fail to describe the Way, nor that it is beyond the realm of mind and consciousness.
Since names and signs are absent, fetters and delusions do not arise; thus, there is no birth and death.
It cannot be destroyed.
Because it is extinguished and utterly ceased, it is called "cessation that transcends dependence.
Because inverted perceptions are severed, it is called "contemplation that transcends dependence."
This is also the cessation-and-contemplation that transcends all existence,
up to the cessation-and-contemplation that transcends birth and death;
this cessation-and-contemplation that transcends all dependence is ultimately ineffable.
If there are causes and conditions for the four *siddhāntas*, it may also be taught accordingly.
If there are causes and conditions related to the world (*loka*), one teaches by accommodating differences.
If there are causes and conditions related to individuals (*pudgala*), one teaches by integrating the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
If there are causes and conditions involving counteraction, they are explained in terms of mutual dependence;

if there are causes and conditions pertaining to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they are explained as being beyond all dependence. This explanation is for the purpose of establishing calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
This name does not exist within, without, or in between the two;
nor does it possess inherent existence.
This name neither abides, nor does it not abide.
This word does not exist within the four horizontal propositions or the four vertical propositions;
therefore, it is said that this word does not abide.
Nor does it exist within that which is neither horizontal nor vertical.
Therefore, it is said that words neither abide nor do not abide,
because these characters are unattainable. Thus,
it is called "cessation and contemplation beyond dependence."
It is also called the inconceivable śamatha-vipaśyanā;
it is also called the non-arising śamatha-vipaśyanā;
it is also called the śamatha-vipaśyanā of the one great matter.
Therefore, such a great matter is not contrasted with a small matter;
it is like how space is not called "great" because of a small space.
It is the same with *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
It is not because of delusion and confusion that it is called "calm abiding and insight" (śamatha-vipaśyanā).
Since there is nothing with which it can be contrasted, as it is the solitary Dharma-realm,
it is therefore called "absolute calm abiding and insight."
Worldly people attempt to explain the meaning of "absolute transcendence" through various verbal formulations,
yet they ultimately fail to attain it. Why is this?
Ordinary minds race with thoughts, engaging in various calculations and deliberations,
discriminating between awakening and non-awakening, mind and non-mind,
and the distinctions between ordinary beings and sages.
When there is cessation, one depends upon non-cessation;
the inconceivable depends upon the conceivable.
As these revolutions depend upon one another, when they are utterly ceased, there is nowhere for them to lodge.
If one attains the meaning, words vanish and the movements of the mind are also severed.
Following wisdom, there is wondrous awakening, and no further conceptual discrimination.
One neither speaks of awakening nor non-awakening, nor of the noble nor the non-noble; the mind does not engage in thought or deliberation regarding the inconceivable and so forth.
Various deluded thoughts that differentiate based on principles are all termed "relative.
When true wisdom is developed, it transcends all such relativities.
When it is cut off, it is again cut off.
As previously stated, fire and wood are termed "mutually dependent" (*juedai*).
Therefore, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra says:
All phenomena do not wait for one another;
this is because they do not abide for even a single thought-moment.
This is precisely that meaning.
If that were so, then being free from all dependencies would be the realm of the sages alone,
and the initial stage of the path would have no part in it.
Now, if we view this through the lens of the six stages of realization (*liuji*),
the initial aspiration loses nothing of its essence, and the sacred realm is not confused with the mundane.
As for the differences between the three assemblies:
Such cessation-and-contemplation, being free from all dependence,
is also called inconceivable and is also called great.
The Great Sūtra states: "Great" means inconceivable.
In other sūtras and śāstras, it is sometimes termed "detachment."
Alternatively, it is called non-abiding, non-attachment, the unconditioned, and quiescent extinction;
it is the non-differentiation of meditative concentration,
relinquishment, equanimity, and so forth— all such terms as these are synonyms for *śamatha*.
Cessation (*śamatha*) is already a supreme, inconceivable greatness;
detachment (*viveka*) and so forth are all likewise supreme, inconceivable greatnesses.

In other contexts, these may be termed knowledge (*jñāna*), vision (*darśana*), clarity (*vidyā*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), the eye (*cakṣus*), awakening (*bodha*), wisdom (*prajñā*), illumination (*avabhāsa*), realization (*parijñā*), penetration (*prativedha*), and so on.
All of these are merely different names for contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Since contemplation is itself utterly great and inconceivable,
so too are knowledge, vision, and the rest utterly great and inconceivable.
Why is this? Prajñā is a single dharma, yet the Buddha speaks of it by various names;
liberation is likewise so.
Though there are many names,
they are like space— non-existent, immovable, and unobstructed.
One should know that the three virtues are in fact but a single dharma.
According to the various classes of sentient beings, different names have been established for it.
If you hear of its absolute transcendence, be careful not to be startled or afraid;
if you hear of its inclusion of all differences, be careful not to harbor doubts or let yourself be harmed.
Furthermore, regarding the convergence of the specific characteristics of śamatha and vipaśyanā:
śamatha is also called vipaśyanā and is also called non-cessation;
vipaśyanā is also called śamatha and is also called non-contemplation.
This is identical in meaning to the previous explanation of the name.
○ Fourth, regarding the three virtues:
if the various different names found in the various sutras all refer to *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, then...
If names are immeasurable and their meanings are likewise immeasurable,
for what reason are cessation and contemplation explained by means of only three meanings?
It is simply to provide this explanation in correspondence with the three virtues.
All phenomena (*dharma*) are immeasurable.
For what reason, then, are they specifically correlated with only these three virtues?
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
From the first generation of the mind of enlightenment, the bodhisattva constantly contemplates nirvana while practicing the path.
As the Mahāyāna Sūtra says:
"Both Buddhas and sentient beings are all established within the secret treasury."
The secret is precisely nirvāṇa;
nirvāṇa is precisely the three virtues;
the three virtues are precisely cessation and contemplation.
Since both oneself and others, as well as the beginning and the end, can all attain entry through cultivation,
these [terms] are employed in contrast to one another.
If two characters were used to apply universally to the three virtues, [the distinction would be lost].
Calm abiding (*śamatha*) is itself abandonment; this abandonment universally leads to liberation.
Insight (*vipaśyanā*) is itself wisdom; this wisdom universally leads to *prajñā*.
The equality of calm abiding and insight is termed the characteristic of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The characteristic of relinquishment (prahāṇa-nimitta) penetrates the Dharma-body.
Furthermore, tranquility (śamatha) is śamatha,
and insight (vipaśyanā) is vipaśyanā.
Because of those [qualities], it is *udāsīna* (indifferent).
It pervades the three *guṇas* as previously described.

Furthermore, it is precisely through inconceivable *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* that one attains the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Moreover, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies the eighteen kinds of emptiness as an exposition of *prajñā*,
and the hundred and eight *samādhis* as an exposition of *dhyāna*.
Although there are these two preceding and succeeding interpretations,
how could it be that dhyāna lacks prajñā or prajñā lacks dhyāna?
It is simply that non-duality manifests as duality, and duality is itself non-duality.
Non-duality is the Dharmakāya;
duality consists of meditative concentration and wisdom.
These three dharmas have never been separated from one another.
Therefore, a great sutra states:
"The Buddha-nature has five names;
it is sometimes called Śūraṅgama and sometimes called Prajñā."
Now, it is neither cessation nor contemplation;
yet what is sometimes called cessation and sometimes called contemplation is precisely inconceivable cessation and contemplation.
This penetrates the three inconceivable virtues.
Furthermore, regarding how cessation and contemplation each penetrate the three virtues:
within cessation there is contemplation, and within contemplation there is cessation.
The tranquility that is the cessation of stillness is virtuous stillness, subsumed under the category of concentration (*samādhi*),
which also extends to liberation (*vimokṣa*).
The tranquility that is the cessation of activity is virtuous activity, subsumed under the category of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
This immediately encompasses Prajñā;
it is not merely cessation, for cessation belongs to the category of Principle (li).
This immediately encompasses the Dharmakāya.
Its meaning is evident.
Penetrating contemplation is subsumed within the gate of wholesome concentration of cessation;
it thus leads to liberation.
The contemplation of penetration is subsumed under the gate of contemplating wholesome conduct;
it thus pervades *prajñā*. The contemplation that is not [conceptual] contemplation is subsumed under the contemplation of principle.
This directly refers to the Dharma-body;
this meaning may also be seen [in other texts].
Furthermore, regarding the fact that cessation (śamatha) and contemplation (vipaśyanā) are common to the three virtues:
Cessation (śamatha) and penetration (vipaśyanā) both derive their names from that which they abandon;
they thus encompass liberation (vimokṣa).
The cessation of both śamatha and vipaśyanā, as well as their ultimate realization, all derive their names from the wisdom that takes them as objects;
thus they are subsumed within prajñā.
It is not that śamatha is merely "stopping" nor that vipaśyanā is merely "contemplating"—both are designated as *dharmatā*.
This refers to the Dharma-body.
Furthermore, regarding the three virtues (triguṇa) being common to both śamatha and vipaśyanā,
it is because these three virtues are equally shared by the two characters [śamatha and vipaśyanā].
Furthermore, each of the three virtues should correspond to two characters.
Regarding the commonality of the three virtues: liberation corresponds to both tranquility (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā).
Prajñā (wisdom) is universally characterized by contemplation;
the Dharma-body is universally characterized by being neither cessation nor contemplation;
and the three virtues are each universally characterized by both cessation and contemplation.
Now, as for liberation, it is fully endowed with liberation.
It possesses three kinds:
the purification through skillful means, liberation, and the thorough cessation of stilling.
The liberation of perfect purity (pariśuddha-vimukti) encompasses both cessation (nirodha) and non-cessation (anirodha);
the liberation of natural purity (prakṛti-viśuddha-vimukti) encompasses both non-cessation and non-non-cessation.
Now, as for prajñā, it is the complete perfection of prajñā.
There are three types:
the prajñā of the knowledge of the path (mārgajñatā) penetrates and discerns;
the prajñā of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā) universally observes and thoroughly penetrates.
The wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the prajñā-pāramitā are neither contemplation nor non-contemplation;
the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is likewise fully endowed with three kinds [of aspects].
The form-body (*rūpakāya*), however, consists of one stillness and one contemplation.
The Dharma-gate body penetrates both cessation and contemplation as one;
the reality-body penetrates both cessation and contemplation as one;
the meaning of this is evident.
If one has faith that the Three Virtues are supremely and inconceivably great,
then once the general principle is clarified,
one must likewise believe that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are supremely and inconceivably great.
If one believes that the three dharmas are fully present in nirvāṇa, it is called the Secret Treasury;
likewise, if one believes that the three kinds of cessation are fully present, it is called Great Tranquil Samādhi and named the Secret Treasury;
and if one believes that the three kinds of contemplation are fully present, it is called Great Wisdom and named the Secret Treasury.
Furthermore, to have faith that the three dharmas— neither cessation nor contemplation— are fully present is called the Secret Treasury.

If one has faith that the three virtues are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither unified nor separate, like the three dots or the three eyes [of the Buddha], then one possesses true understanding.
One also believes that the three stops and three contemplations are neither sequential nor simultaneous, neither unified nor distinct;
yet, various sutras, in accordance with specific conditions, single out one particular dharma to illustrate the fundamental principle.
Just as the Śūraṅgama Samādhi specifically highlights the aspect of cessation (*śamatha*),
yet cessation itself encompasses all phenomena without deficiency,
it is also called the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyagarbha*).
The *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* specifically cite the aspect of contemplation;
yet this contemplation encompasses all phenomena without omission.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* cites the three dharmas as being fully complete.
The Dharma is not many;
it is also called the Secret Treasury.
This is likewise true for śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Whether they open or close,
they neither open much nor close little;
each and every one is the Dharma-realm that encompasses all phenomena.
All are called the Secret Treasury;
if this is so even when citing them individually,
how much more so when citing them collectively?
Since it is thus that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* pervade the three virtues,
so too do they pervade various synonymous terms such as "separation" (*viveka*), "knowledge" (*jñāna*), and "vision" (*darśana*).
Furthermore, they pervade all three names.
That which is called the three types of awakening (trividha-bodhi), the three Buddha-natures (tri-buddhadhātu),
and the Three Jewels (triratna)— all such triads of dharmas are likewise so.
Question:
What is meant by the vertical and horizontal aspects of the meaning of syllables?
What is meant by the meaning of syllables being neither vertical nor horizontal? Answer:
The teachers of the various Hīnayāna schools say that although the prajñā and the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) are already perfected,
the bonds of the fruit still remain.
Liberation is not yet fully realized and the body still relies on impure food;
furthermore, it is subject to impermanence.
One is superior and the other inferior, comparable to a fire spreading across a river.
Furthermore, it is said:
first there is the body endowed with the marks and signs of excellence,
and subsequently one attains the prajñā of the knowledge of all modes.
Only after the subsequent cessation of the body and wisdom does liberation become fully realized.
Since there is thus a sense of superior and inferior, as well as prior and posterior,
it may be compared to three dots of water arranged vertically.
If one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), there is the body but no consciousness;
an Arhat in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) possesses consciousness but no body;
and if one enters the nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa), there is only solitary liberation.
These meanings are each unrelated to one another;
taken side by side they are horizontal,
and stacked one upon another they are vertical.
When these are distinguished,
they differ. The masters of the Mahāyāna teach that the dharmakāya is the primary essence.
Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, this has existed inherently from the beginning;
it is not something that has only arisen now.
It is the liberating cause of *prajñā* (wisdom) and the unconditioned liberation.
These two shall exist across the separation of lifetimes and the transition between worlds, pervading both the pure and the defiled.
This is the vertical meaning of these characters.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The three virtues (guṇas) have no sequence of before or after; they are fully present as a single essence.
It is only from the perspective of their functions that they appear as three distinct entities."
This is simply because the substance is horizontal while the meaning is vertical;
yet it is also said that both substance and meaning are not different.
Yet there is a distinction between concealment and manifestation.
If both are not distinct, one cannot avoid being horizontal;
if concealment and manifestation are distinct, one cannot avoid being vertical.
The various explanations of the Śākyas accord with the sūtras in this way.
Now, it is clarified that the three virtues are all inconceivable; why then do you allow them to be [viewed] vertically?
Why do you suddenly allow them to be [viewed] horizontally?
All are inconceivable *nayuta*s;
all are inconceivable *nayuta*s. This is an explanation according to the *li-zang* (principle-treasury).
The body, the constant wisdom, and the perfection of severance—
all these are entirely the Buddha-dharma, without distinction of superiority or inferiority; therefore,
they are not sequential.
The three virtues (triguṇa) are in profound identity with this single Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Outside of the Dharma-realm, where else could there be any other distinct phenomena?
Therefore, they are not horizontal.
Because it can establish various [distinctions], it is not one;
because it converges in the same ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is not different.
This is an explanation based on the causes of practice.
Because it is three within oneness, it is not horizontal;
because it is one within three, it is not vertical;
because it is three without being three, it is not one.
Because it is not one, it is one; therefore, it is not different.
This is an explanation based on the function of the character.
Such is the meaning of the true letter *i*.
Question:
What is the meaning of the three virtues and the four virtues? Answer:
In general discussion, each of the three virtues is eternally blissful, self, and pure.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra states:
"That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma."
Because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal.
The Dharma is the Dharmakāya;
the Buddha is Prajñā and Vimukti.
Therefore, I have provided this comprehensive explanation.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra states:
"By the cessation of this form, one attains eternal form."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise thus;
therefore, the Dharma-body is entirely eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
The two virtues are also thus.
If one relies on a single mode of transformation, matter is transformed into the Dharma-body;
the Dharma-body, characterized by permanence and bliss, transforms the perceptions of consciousness into prajñā.
This prajñā is itself purity.
The transformation of sensation and mental formations results in liberation; liberation is the self.
Furthermore, based on the foundations of mindfulness, the transformation of consciousness results in permanence.
They transform sensation into pleasure;
they transform perception and formations into a self;
and they transform form into purity.
Thus, there are two interpretations for both the general and specific [aspects]:
"based on the perfect" (yuan) signifies the sudden (dun),
while "based on the distinct" (bie) signifies the gradual (jian), and so forth.
Question:
The three obstructions and the three paths all obstruct the three virtues.
When the three obstructions are opened and cleared away, one reaches the ultimate.
The three paths and four inversions should also be opened up to reach the ultimate.
Answer: By analogy.
What are they? There are three kinds of karma:
namely, tainted karma (*sāsrava-karma*), untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*), and karma that is neither tainted nor untainted.
One is moved by the three types of retribution—

namely, the retribution of segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*), the provisional retribution (*upāya-bhava*), and the true retribution (*dharmatā-bhava*). These retributions arise from three kinds of afflictions (*kleśa*).
This refers to the grasping of signs, which is the dust-like sands of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Furthermore, regarding each of the three types of retribution, one opens up three paths;
likewise, regarding the three types of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Each of these opens up the four inversions.
Third, regarding the explanation of the essence and characteristics of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*:
since the general meaning has already been understood as expansive as described above.
The names are vast and remote, as if pointing toward something;
one must recognize that the essence and principle are profound and mysterious.
To roughly manifest this essence, I shall rely upon four points.
First, the characteristics of the teachings;
second, vision and wisdom;
third, the objective realm.
Fourth, gain and loss.
Now, principle relies upon the teachings for its manifestation;
since the teachings are manifold, they employ signs to make them clear.
Because there are differences in the ways of entering into principle, it is manifested through vision and wisdom.
Because the truths possess both provisional and ultimate aspects, they are manifested through their objective spheres.
Because there are distinctions among persons regarding their convergence [with the truth], they are manifested through gain and loss.
The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) uses the "Fourfold Unity" to clarify the Reality;
now, by means of the "Four Sections," the Essence is revealed.
These two approaches may be considered analogous.
Regarding the clarification of the characteristics of the teaching:
Now, the names "calm abiding" (śamatha) and "insight" (vipaśyanā) apply to both ordinary beings and sages;
one must not seek their distinct essential natures by relying solely on these common designations.
Therefore, they are distinguished by their characteristics:
if an ordinary person’s cessation of unwholesome states is that which is to be remedied, it is the characteristic of *śamatha*;
if the arising of wholesome states through practice is present, it is the characteristic of *vipaśyanā*.
Furthermore, the four dhyānas and the four immeasurable minds are the characteristics of śamatha;
the six practices are the characteristics of vipaśyanā.
All of these have not yet escaped birth and death.
That is to say, having outflows (*sāsrava*) constitutes its characteristic. Thus, the *Mahā-śāstra* states:
"Apart from Mount Malaya, there is nowhere else from which sandalwood emerges."
Apart from the wisdom of the three vehicles, there is no other true wisdom;
therefore, it is not what is being discussed here.
As for the two vehicles, they possess the nine notions, the ten notions, the eight liberations, and the nine successive attainments.
For the most part, this consists of the aspect of quiescence (*śamatha*) that proceeds by way of mere cessation;
there is also the aspect of insight (*vipaśyanā*) consisting of wisdom regarding the Four Noble Truths.
Although this *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* brings one out of birth and death, it is a coarse means of deliverance.
By extinguishing form, one enters emptiness.
This emptiness may also be called "cessation" (śamatha),
and it may also be called "neither cessation nor non-cessation."
Yet it cannot be called "contemplation.
Why? Because the body is reduced to ashes and wisdom is extinguished, it is not called contemplation.
However, the analysis of phenomena (dharmapravicaya) as the characteristic of the outflow-free state is not what is being discussed here;
there are only three types of skillful cessation: first, cessation through realizing the true nature (tattvārtha-śamatha).
Second is the cessation that accords with conditions through skillful means;
third is the cessation that quiets the discrimination of the two extremes;
fourth is the cessation that realizes the true essence.
All phenomena arise from conditions;
their causes and conditions are empty and without a master.
One who quiets the mind and reaches the fundamental source is therefore called a śramaṇa.
Because one knows that the nature of dependent origination is a provisional conjunction and an illusory transformation, it is called "substance" (*tǐ*).
When the deluded thoughts that grasp at objects cease upon attaining emptiness,
and emptiness itself is the truth, it is termed "stopping in the truth of substance" (*zhēnzhǐ*).
Second, regarding "stopping according with conditions through expedient means":
if the three vehicles equally enter the truth by severing afflictions through the path of wordlessness,
then that truth is not different.
It is simply said that afflictions and their residual habits (vāsanā) may be either exhausted or not exhausted.
If the two vehicles realize the truth and do not require expedient means to bring them to rest,
the Bodhisattva enters into the conventional realm and should correctly engage in its practical application.
Because one knows that emptiness is not [inherently] empty, it is called "expedient means" (upāya).
Because one discriminates between medicines and illnesses, it is called "according with conditions" (anupratyaya).
Because the mind rests in conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), it is called "calming" (śamatha).
The Sūtra’s statement that “the mind remains constant whether in motion or at rest” also serves to verify this meaning.
Regarding the cessation of the dualistic discrimination of the three breaths:
there is the flux of birth and death, and the assurance of Nirvāṇa.
All these involve partial practice and partial application, failing to realize the Middle Way.
Now one knows that the mundane is not mundane, for it is quiescent at the limit of the mundane;
yet one does not attain a state of quiescence at the limit of emptiness that is non-mundane.
This is called "stopping that quiets the two extremes.
Although these three types of stopping have not been seen in the sūtras or śāstras,
they are established as names according to their meaning in correspondence with the three types of contemplation.
The *Śāstra* states:
"When a bodhisattva, relying on and following the scriptural teachings, provides designations [for them],
this is called the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*)."
Establishing these names is without fault.
If one can seek out the meaning from the sutras and obtain these names, they will immediately correspond perfectly with this principle.
Upon careful examination, these three types of cessation (*śamatha*) are similar in their essential character to the previous explanation of the names.
Their characteristics differ.
That which is the same is that both cessation and semblance-cessation resemble the realization of reality.
Cessation that resembles expedient means follows conditions;
cessation that resembles the stilling of the two extremes differs in its characteristics, namely, the characteristics of the three truths.
The first three establish the next three;
the last one possesses all three. Why is this so?
When, during the practice of "stopping by realizing the essence," one penetrates that causes and conditions are merely provisional names, empty, without self, and that the flow of evil has ceased,
this is called the meaning of "stopping.
To settle the mind upon principle is precisely to penetrate causes and conditions.
This is the meaning of cessation.
This principle is itself the truth, and the truth is itself the source.
The source is neither subject to cessation nor non-cessation.
This is the cessation of cessation.
These three meanings together constitute the characteristics of the true cessation of the essence.
When one employs the cessation of skillful means, the illumination of the provisional is sovereign.
The cessation of distraction and ignorance is the meaning of "stopping" (śamatha).
Stilling the mind through provisional principles is like the Vimalakīrti entering samādhi to observe the faculties and natures of monks, thereby distinguishing between medicines and ailments.
This is the meaning of cessation.
The immovability of the provisional principle is not the cessation of cessation.
Thus, these three meanings together constitute the characteristics of the expedient means of "cessation according with conditions."
When the two extremes are stilled, the two characteristics of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are both stilled;
this is the meaning of "stopping" (śamatha).
The *prajñā* that enters into principle is called the Middle Way dwelling within the mind that takes [reality] as its object.
This is the meaning of cessation.
This principle of the true mark is neither ceasing nor not ceasing;
it is the meaning of non-cessation as cessation.
These three meanings together establish the characteristics of "stopping" (*śamatha*) that avoids the two extremes; thus, they are fundamentally different from the previous [explanation].
Furthermore, this is not what is employed here. Next, the characteristics of "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) are clarified.
There are three types of contemplation.
Entering emptiness from the conventional is called the contemplation of the two truths;
entering the conventional from emptiness is called the contemplation of equality.
Taking these two contemplations as the path of skillful means, one enters the Middle Way that simultaneously illuminates both truths.
With each thought-moment becoming tranquil and extinguished, one naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
This is called the contemplation of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way.
This is what is called the "Two Truths" as taught in the *Ratnavyuha-sūtra* (Yingluo jing).
Contemplating the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) serves as the means for entering emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and emptiness is realized through that means.
Because the subject and object are discussed together, it is termed the "contemplation of the Two Truths."
Furthermore, on the day one realizes emptiness, one not only perceives emptiness but also recognizes the provisional.
Just as when clouds are cleared away, what was obscured above becomes manifest and what was below becomes bright,
through the simultaneous realization of the provisional and the true, this constitutes the contemplation of the two truths.
Now, since one attains the ultimate by means of the conventional, for what reason is this not considered the contemplation of the two truths?
Furthermore, the conventional is that which is to be refuted, while the ultimate is that which is employed.
If it were based on that which is refuted, one should speak of it as the contemplation of conventional truth.
If one follows its actual function, it should be called "contemplation of ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-satya*).
However, because the function and the negation are discussed in conjunction, it is called "contemplation of the two truths" (*dvaya-satya*).
Furthermore, there are three types of analytical discernment (*vikalpa*).
First, regarding the teaching, there is the contemplation of the two truths according to sentiment;
regarding practice, there is the contemplation of the two truths according to sentiment and wisdom;
regarding realization, there is the contemplation of the two truths according to wisdom.
Although the merit of the initial contemplation has not yet accorded with ultimate truth, one may attain the contemplation of the two truths according to the teachings and their practice. Question:
Should the function of the initial contemplation’s refutation be given its own name?
The second contemplation also refutes function.
Should it also be said that there are two truths? Answer:
Although the names of the two truths were previously accepted and subsequently refuted in their functional application,
they are here again accepted under the name of "equality" from the perspective of the most excellent [truth].
Question:
Question: Since the third contemplation also refutes function (*kāritra*), why is it not given a name derived from its excellence?
Answer: Because the preceding two contemplations were subject to stagnation, they required further refutation and further application.
The third contemplation, "Non-obstruction," receives its name solely from its function;
it cannot be treated as an identical case [with the others]. Question:
Question: Since the first two contemplations both contemplate the two truths, they should also both enter into the two truths.
Answer: The first is for the purpose of destroying afflictions; therefore, it contemplates the conventional (the provisional).
Because one employs the true, one contemplates the true;
therefore, both are contemplated.
Because one employs [one] while not employing [the other], they do not enter together.
Question:
Both the ultimate and the conventional are designated as *satya* (truths).
However, since the conventional within and outside the realms (*dhātu*) is not [ultimately] rational, how can it be called a truth?
Answer: The *Bhūmivastu* clarifies two natures of phenomena:
first, the nature of things (*vastudharmatā*), and second, the nature of distinctions (*viśeṣadharmatā*).
Because the nature of the two realities is the true reality itself,
it is an alternative name for the two truths;
since both are designated as "dharma-nature" (dharmatā).
For what reason can they not both be designated as "truths"?
Question: If that is so, why can they both be designated as "nirvāṇa"? Answer:
The Sūtra says:
"A poor man obtains treasure," and so on, up to "a monkey obtains wine.
Furthermore, the station of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the mundane nirvāṇa.
This is precisely its meaning.
Question:
If that is so, are both of them untainted (*anāsrava*)?
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* replies:
"Worldly right view and supramundane right view. Question: [What is the distinction between them?]
If that is so, are both then without arising?
The answer is:
The Sūtra says:
"Different phenomena are mutually non-existent.
Question:
"In entering emptiness from the conventional, must one necessarily destroy the conventional in order to enter emptiness?"
Answer: Generally speaking, there should be four permutations;
it does not contradict [the definition of] entry.
Penetration and non-penetration;
non-penetration and non-non-penetration.
This continues up to thirty-six phrases as explained below.
Regarding the "equal contemplation that enters the provisional from emptiness":
if one has entered emptiness, since there is not even emptiness to be found, what provisional [designation] could there be to enter?
One should know that this contemplation is for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
Because one knows the true and the non-true as skillful means for emerging into the provisional, it is said to "proceed from emptiness.
Because one distinguishes between medicines and illnesses without error, it is said to "enter the provisional."
"Equanimity" (平等) is called "equanimity" in comparison to what precedes it.
In the preceding contemplation, one destroys the illness of the provisional by not employing provisional dharmas but employing only true dharmas.
To destroy the one [provisional] while not destroying the other [true] is not yet equanimity.
Subsequently, one contemplates the breaking of the illness of emptiness by returning to the use of conventional dharmas;
since the breaking and the application are equal when viewed from different perspectives, they are said to be "equal.
This shall now be illustrated by analogy.
It is like a blind person who has first regained their sight and sees the sky and forms;
although they see these forms, they cannot distinguish between the various kinds of herbs, trees, roots, stalks, branches, leaves, medicines, or poisons.
When entering emptiness from the conventional according to wisdom,
one likewise perceives the two truths but cannot employ the conventional.
It is like a person whose eyes have opened and can thus see both emptiness and form.
One immediately understands the categories of consciousness and thoroughly comprehends causes and conditions;
whether coarse or subtle, medicinal or dietary, all are recognized as consciousness and employed for the benefit of others.
This is an analogy for entering the conventional from emptiness, wherein both the ultimate and the conventional are truly real.
Applying oneself correctly to the conventional for the sake of transforming sentient beings is therefore called "entering the conventional.
It is further described as "equanimity."
The meaning is as previously explained.
Regarding the contemplation of the Middle Way and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*):
the previous contemplation of the provisional emptiness was the emptiness of saṃsāra.
Subsequently, one contemplates that the emptiness of emptiness is itself the emptiness of nirvāṇa;
this dual negation of the two extremes is called the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness as the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga), through which one attains the middle way.
Therefore, it is said that the mind and mental factors are quiescent and flow into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Furthermore, first observing through the function of emptiness and subsequently observing through the function of the provisional is the skillful means of maintaining both simultaneously.
When entering the Middle Way, one is able to simultaneously illuminate both truths.
Thus, a sutra says:
"If the mind is in meditative concentration, one can know the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of worldly phenomena."
The meaning of the two preceding contemplations lies in these two kinds of skillful means (*upāya*).
Question:
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
Question: Why is it that those with an excess of concentration or an excess of wisdom both fail to see the Buddha-nature? Answer:
Next, in the third contemplation, the followers of the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching possess the first stage of contemplation;
this belongs to those who have more concentration and less wisdom, and thus do not see the Buddha-nature.
The Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching possess the second stage of contemplation.
Those who possess an abundance of wisdom but a deficiency in meditative concentration likewise do not perceive the Buddha-nature.

Question:
The Sūtra states that Bodhisattvas of the ten stages see [reality] not clearly because they rely on the wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus).
It is not that they do not see at all;
the first contemplation is the stage of the wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus),
and the second contemplation is the stage of the dharma-eye (dharma-cakṣus).
"How can you say that both eyes see nothing at all?
He replied,
"The Buddha rebuked those who rely sequentially on one-sided concentration and one-sided wisdom."
It cannot be said that they see; as for what is called "seeing with the wisdom-eye," its name is the same,
but in reality it refers to the stage of the ten abidings in the Perfect Teaching.
When the three contemplations manifest before one and one enters the principle of the three truths,
this is called "abiding" (*sthiti*). This state of abiding is termed the "eye of wisdom."
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "May I obtain, like the World-Honored One, the supreme purity of the eye of wisdom.
Such an eye of wisdom perceives only partially and incompletely;
thus it is said that it is like seeing forms at night, such as geese and swans in the sky.
The wisdom-eye of the two vehicles does not attain such a name.
Therefore, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is said: "For example, suppose there is a person who digs into a high plateau and sees only dry earth;
yet, as he continues his labor without ceasing, he eventually sees moist earth."
Thus, one gradually reaches the mud and subsequently obtains water.
Dry soil is a metaphor for the first contemplation;
moist soil is a metaphor for the second contemplation.
Mud is a metaphor for the third contemplation;
water is a metaphor for the perfect and sudden contemplation,
and it is also a metaphor for the teaching.
The Tripiṭaka Teaching does not elucidate the Middle Way, like dry soil; the Shared Teaching is like damp soil;
the Distinct Teaching is like mud;
and the Perfect Teaching elucidates the Middle Way, like water.
It is that which cannot be elucidated by the two teachings and to which the two practices do not reach.
How could the eye of wisdom, which perceives only partial emptiness, ever perceive one's nature?
If it were to perceive one's nature, such a thing would be impossible.
These three contemplations share the same names as the previous three, yet their meanings and characteristics differ.
The similarity is that the former were penetrating contemplations of all that is illusory, appearing to be an entry from the conventional into emptiness.
Previously, one contemplates that principle is harmonized by principle and phenomena are harmonized by phenomena;
this resembles entering the contemplation of equality within the conventional.
Previously, one does not contemplate; this resembles the Middle Way.
As for their differing characteristics:

the former consists of the characteristic of one truth, while the latter consists of the characteristic of three truths; furthermore, the former three contemplations collectively accomplish the latter three, and the latter three fully possess the former three.
Why is this so? For instance,
entering from the conventional into emptiness to shatter the massive rock of the four abidings—
does this not constitute the meaning of "puncturing through"?
The emptiness of the very emptiness that is entered is itself the principle (*tattva*).
Wisdom is that which manifests the principle;
it is the realization of the meaning through contemplation.
This principle of emptiness is precisely the meaning of non-contemplation as contemplation.
These three meanings together constitute the characteristics of entering the contemplation of emptiness.
Entering the provisional from emptiness likewise possesses these three meanings.
Why is this? Because the dharma of the conventional designation "consciousness" destroys the obstacle of ignorance;
this is precisely the meaning of "pervading."
To illuminate the principle of conventional designations (prajñapti) without error through discernment is precisely the meaning of "contemplative penetration" (vipaśyanā).
Since the principle of the conventional is eternally thus, it is the meaning of "non-contemplation" within contemplation.
These three meanings together constitute the characteristics of the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*).
The contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) likewise possesses these three meanings.
To be empty of the two extremes is precisely the meaning of "pervasion" (*vyāpti*).
Entering the Middle Way correctly is the meaning of "penetrating through observation.
The dharma-nature of the Middle Way is the meaning of "observation that is not observation.
These three meanings together constitute the characteristics of the contemplation of the Middle Way.

Question:
Regarding "seeing with the eye" and "knowing through wisdom," are knowing and seeing different?
Answer: This should be analyzed through four propositions (catuṣkoṭi):
that which is knowledge but not vision, and that which is vision but not knowledge.
It is both known and seen, yet it is not known and not seen.
Because ordinary beings have not realized it, they do not see it;
because they have not heard it, they do not know it.
Because those of the two vehicles have realized it, they also see it;
because they have heard of it, they also know it.
Because Pratyekabuddhas have realized it, this is seeing.
Because they have not heard it, they do not know it;

He performs the Buddha-work by bringing sentient beings to maturity.
Subsequently, while seated at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he exhausts the afflictions of views and thought through thirty-four moments of mind.
These are the thirty-four moments of mind.
The eight patiences, the eight knowledges, the nine unhindered knowledges,
and the nine liberations together constitute thirty-four moments of mind.
Furthermore, the Sūtra says:
In a single thought-moment, there are six hundred births and cessations.
The masters of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* say that one thought-moment consists of sixty *kṣaṇas*.
It is simply that by means of a single thought, one enters from the conventional into emptiness and attains the eye of wisdom;
by illuminating the ultimate truth, one attains Buddhahood.
Having already illuminated the conventional, one next again illuminates the ultimate.

Regarding the simultaneous elucidation of the two truths: disciples differ from bodhisattvas in that bodhisattvas illuminate only the conventional and not the ultimate, whereas those of the two vehicles illuminate only the ultimate and not the conventional;
only the Buddha is able to encompass both.
Furthermore, regarding the ultimate truth of the Middle Way:
the Tripitaka and the two truths are already skillful means;
upon these two truths, one further adds the Middle Way.
Beyond the skillful means, there are further skillful means:
one perceives these truths with the Buddha-eye;
because of knowing these truths, one further attains the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
When separated, there are two; when combined, there are three.
This constitutes the characteristics of the separation and combination of the Two Truths and Three Truths within the Dharma of the Tripiṭaka.
Next, those of the Three Vehicles alike employ the path beyond words to sever afflictions.

Regarding the discussion on the convergence and divergence of the truths: they are identical according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), but distinct according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
There are two kinds of emptiness:
first, mere emptiness;
second, not-mere-emptiness.
The Great Sūtra states:
"Those of the Two Vehicles perceive only emptiness and do not perceive non-emptiness;
the wise, however, not only perceive emptiness but are also able to perceive non-emptiness."
Non-emptiness is Great Nirvāṇa.
The wisdom of the followers of the Two Vehicles is merely empty, like a firefly;
the wisdom of the Bodhisattvas is like the sun.
Since emptiness and discernment are distinct, there would otherwise be a distinction between two truths;
yet now they are unified as a single True Truth.
Those of the Two Vehicles realize the conventional and enter the True.
One merely enters emptiness alone and cannot proceed from that emptiness into the provisional;
thus, one lacks the function of transforming others.
The Bodhisattva, however, realizes the provisional and enters into true emptiness.
They are able to enter the provisional from mere emptiness to transform and deliver sentient beings and purify Buddha-lands;
bodhisattvas of superior capacity realize the provisional and enter the true.
Entering first, one realizes that all is empty;
entering next, one realizes that it is not merely empty.
Thus, one destroys ignorance and perceives the Buddha-nature.
This is a true and eternal parting from what preceded;
how could it be the same single ultimate truth?
Formerly, the School of Adornment (Yogācāra) said:
The fruit of Buddhahood transcends the two truths;
if one attempts to establish a doctrinal interpretation based on this partial understanding, it will not succeed,
for one would not know what distinct object the Buddha’s wisdom illuminates.
What specific afflictions are severed?
If one adopts the meaning of "attaining the present intention" as being "going outside," then [the argument] is established.
The Kai-shan school says:
The fruit of Buddhahood does not exist outside the two truths;
it cannot move beyond or differ from those of the two vehicles,
and its conceptual definition would likewise fail to be established.
If one attains this intent, even the meaning of non-emergence is established.
Since antiquity, this has been called the "refined elegance" (fengliu) of the two truths; the intent lies herein.
It is not merely emptiness, but emptiness in conjunction with [the conventional].
It is simply the One True Truth;
when separated, it becomes two true truths,
which differs from the approach of the Tripiṭaka masters.
In that Tripiṭaka, the third truth consists merely of the name "Middle Way" and has no separate essence;
the eye has no separate seeing.
Wisdom has no separate object of cognition; now it is not so.
The third truth is also called the Truth of Reality (bhūtārtha-satya).
It is also called the Middle Way and the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya).
It possesses a distinct substance, a distinct vision, and a distinct knowledge;
this constitutes the characteristics of the union and separation of the two truths and three truths in the Shared Teaching (pāryāyika-yāna).
Next, the Separate Teaching (biejiao) clarifies the two truths, distinguishing them from the previous [teaching].
The preceding combination of the true and the conventional constitutes the conventional for this school.
"Conventional" refers to the world of distinct and separate phenomena.
The conventional exists and the ultimate does not.
Ordinary beings are subsumed within the conventional truth,
while those of the two vehicles are subsumed within the ultimate truth.
Because there is the distinction between existence and non-existence, it is termed "conventional" (saṃvṛti).
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* refers to those of the two vehicles as "beings whose minds are confused by emptiness.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
When I discourse with Maitreya on the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
the five hundred śrāvakas believe I am speaking of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
If one were to discuss the two truths, the conventional truth would not be revealed.
If one establishes three truths,
the conditioned conventional is opened up and the unconditioned real is opened up;
this is contrasted with "not merely empty," which constitutes the ultimate truth.
This is the characteristic of the separation and integration of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavidyā*).
